evidence.claim: In 1922, Forest Service supervisor Aldo Leopold proposed protecting the river’s headwaters by excluding roads and denying use permits.
evidence.quote: In 1922, Aldo Leopold, a United States Forest Service supervisor of the Carson National Forest proposed that the headwaters area of the Gila River should be preserved by an administrative process of excluding roads and denying use permits.

evidence.claim: His work led to recognition of the Gila as the National Forest System’s first wilderness area in 1924.

flags: Road construction, promoters and designation chronology are not documented in the cache. The middle overview paragraph uses the documented history of road exclusion in the adjoining Gila Wilderness, rather than inventing a history of the byway.

New Mexico Tourism gives 93 miles; FHWA and Wikipedia give 95. Omitted precise length, retained FHWA’s attributed driving allowance. This is not a verified total including the cliff-dwellings excursion.
The tourism page says the byway travels through wilderness; the wilderness page says roads are excluded and the monument is adjacent. Copy distinguishes the forested drive from designated wilderness.

Kept all current moments and metadata. Route order starts at Silver City, rotating the material loop; the cliff dwellings require a separate excursion before the Mimbres leg. Detailed junction routing needs a manager map; cache does not establish current restrictions or closures.

Chino cache dates open-pit operations to 1910; Santa Rita cache says conversion in 1901. Omitted the current draft’s 1910 claim pending resolution. Pinos Altos and Silver City pages also conflict on railway operation dates; omitted them.

No tribal-authored or NPS source is cached for the dwellings. Used restrained physical and tree-ring details, not motives or an abandonment explanation. Omitted the Billy the Kid passage for focus; its facts do appear in the cache.
